newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemenis to vote in parliamentary elections.
newsitem.headline: Yemenis to vote in parliamentary elections.

text.p: Yemen votes on Sunday in parliamentary elections seen as a test of whether the country, which was almost ripped apart in a 1994 civil war, can guarantee the political stability needed to lure foreign investment.

The electorate of about 4.6 million has a choice between 2,306 candidates, including 17 women, standing for the 301 seats under the banner of 12 parties or as independents in the first parliamentary polls since 1993.
Diplomats expect President Ali Abdullah Saleh's ruling General People's Congress (GPC) and its junior coalition partner, the Islamist Islah Party, to win a dominant share of the seats.

But they say the contest could be more interesting than the 1993 elections because the main opposition Yemen Socialist Party (YSP) and three others are boycotting the polls due to alleged irregularities, leaving a vacuum.
Saleh has denied opposition claims that the government had already fixed the elections through multiple registrations by army and security personnel prior to the arrival of international observers.
"In the last elections north and south were thinking about reconciliation. This time it's more a question of political stability," said one election observer.
Western diplomats said the GPC had become increasingly concerned over the growing influence of the Islah Party and tensions appeared to rise between the two in the run-up to the elections.
Political stability is the ingredient needed to ensure more foreign investment in the impoverished Arab state, a small oil producer.
The Republic of Yemen was formed in 1990 by the merger of conservative North Yemen and Marxist South Yemen following hundreds of years of separation.

A secessionist campaign by the south in 1994 was crushed by forces loyal to Saleh. He and other officials say the country is now united, while southern opposition figures say the north has imposed a unity of occupation.

The election battle has largely been fought out in garbage-strewn urban alleys and isolated mountain villages where candidates have made competing promises of more roads, telephone lines and electricity.

"The election will fix the roads and bring projects and water," said Ahmed Ali Hizam, 81, as he made the one hour walk from his mountain village to the bigger village of Kawkaban, about 65 km (40 miles) northwest of Sanaa.

The GPC hopes to win more seats in parliament to gain the political clout needed to press ahead with what many Yemenis say are painful economic reforms agreed with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
The YSP, some of whose former leaders launched the south's separatist drive, held 50 seats in the outgoing assembly dominated by the GPC and Islah.
